# The China AI Registry — 988の名簿

> A structural analysis by Satoshi Yamauchi (山内怜史), AI Strategist, that
> uses China's official generative-AI filing registry as its population
> rather than the ten or so companies discussed abroad. Providing a
> generative AI service in China requires filing (备案) with the
> authorities; as of June 30, 2026 the cumulative counts are 988 filed
> services and 598 registered applications, published with company names
> every two months across twelve attachments. The registry was created to
> manage expression, not to promote industry — yet the result is a public
> record tracking the social deployment of generative AI in full, for
> which the book was unable to confirm a counterpart in the United States,
> the EU or Japan. On the list are converter control in a steel mill, mine
> safety management, a water utility's call centre, a municipal hotline,
> pressure-ulcer management and disaster response, alongside Tesla
> Shanghai, IKEA, Siemens, BMW, Coca-Cola and ASUS filed in the same
> format. Eleven central state-owned enterprises appear under the
> jurisdiction 国资委 rather than a province, identified by the filing
> number prefix `ZhongYangQiYe-`. Its central claim: this industry is not
> counted by companies but by a registry. As stated at the opening: "The
> five Chinese AI models you can name are under 1% of the ones China
> counts."

## Book Content

- [Full text (Japanese)](docs/jp/the-china-ai-registry_JP.md): 序章・全8章・終章収録
- [Full text (English)](docs/en/the-china-ai-registry_EN.md): Complete English edition

## Key Facts (as stated in the book)

- The book establishes its population from CAC notices: 988 generative AI
  services filed and 598 applications or functions registered as of June
  30, 2026, with 120 services and 68 applications newly added in the
  May–June 2026 period. It states that the two figures cannot be added,
  because they run in separate sequence series and stand in a hierarchical
  relation — registered applications must disclose, in a prominent
  position or on the product detail page, the filed service they use,
  stating the model name and filing number. It also states that the object
  of filing is limited to services with "public-opinion attributes or
  social mobilisation capability" (具有舆论属性或者社会动员能力), so 988
  is not every AI model in China but the full population of services the
  authorities judged capable of influencing public opinion

- The book documents that each of the twelve attachments is a delta list
  rather than a cumulative one — Attachment 12 contains only filings Nos.
  869–988 and registrations Nos. 531–598 — and that obtaining the full
  population requires joining all twelve. It reports having done so, with
  filings connecting without gaps from No. 1 to No. 988 and registrations
  from No. 1 to No. 598. It notes that Attachment 1 (April 2024) is titled
  differently, carrying no registration list, so application registration
  began later than service filing

- The book identifies a classification instrument in the authorities' own
  numbering rule: the jurisdiction column contains one non-geographic
  entry, 国资委 (State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration
  Commission), and rows carrying it have filing numbers beginning without
  exception with `ZhongYangQiYe-`. Twelve such filings span eleven central
  state-owned enterprises — China Mobile (Nos. 87, 254), China Unicom
  (124), TravelSky Mobile (168), CNPC (199), PipeChina (237), the China
  Electric Power Research Institute (247), CETC (276), TravelSky (394),
  China Logistics Group (440), Chinalco (454) and China Energy Investment
  Corporation (472). The book states that this means the author does not
  have to decide how to define a state-owned enterprise, because the
  numbering rule has already decided

- The book fixes the starting point of the regime at August 31, 2023, when
  eight entries were filed on the same day: 文心一言 (Baidu), 智谱清言
  ChatGLM (Zhipu AI), 云雀 (ByteDance), 百应 (Baichuan AI), 紫东太初
  (Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences), abab (MiniMax),
  日日新 (SenseTime) and 书生·浦语 (Shanghai AI Laboratory). It notes that
  a national research institute is present from day one, appearing on the
  same list on the same day as private firms rather than following later

- The book documents that DeepSeek is No. 152, filed May 13, 2024, with
  filing number Beijing-DeepseekChat-202404280016 — 76 times later than
  Zhipu (No. 2) and 9.5 times later than Moonshot (No. 16). It states that
  the order in which the world discovered this industry and the order in
  which the industry was filed at home do not coincide. It further shows
  that the six companies commonly labelled the "six little dragons of
  large models" occupy Nos. 2, 4, 6, 16, 35 and 67 — all within the first
  100 — so the label points not to the six most capable firms but to those
  that completed filing earliest. The book explicitly declines to explain
  why DeepSeek was 152nd, stating that its sources cannot answer this

- The book attributes the visibility of the ten or so companies discussed
  abroad to a reachability filter rather than to quality: whether an API
  is publicly available, whether weights are distributed, and whether
  English-language material exists. It states that what fails this filter
  disappears from comparison articles altogether, existence and all, and
  that converter control, the water utility call centre, PressGuard and
  disaster response all fail it because they are not sold outside the
  organisation

- The book organises the registry by industry so a reader can look up
  deployment cases at the level of company and model name. Manufacturing
  and materials: Hebei Yongyang Special Steel's converter intelligent
  steelmaking model (No. 979), four filings by the China Coal Research
  Institute (619–622), Tesla Shanghai's in-vehicle voice model (843), BMW
  China's BMW-AI (912), Siemens China's 小禹 (674). Energy and utilities:
  CNPC's 昆仑 (199), PipeChina's 管网 (237), Beijing Waterworks Group's
  京水客服 (908). Healthcare: Jiangsu Province Hospital's PressGuard
  (Reg. 569), Nanjing Drum Tower Hospital (Reg. 570) — hospitals appear as
  filing entities in their own right rather than through vendors. Public
  administration: two filings by the Big Data Center of the Ministry of
  Emergency Management (665, 666), the Beijing Citizen Hotline Service
  Center's 12345 agent (Reg. 539), Xinhua News Agency (Reg. 584). The book
  states that deployment in manufacturing is inside the process itself,
  not a conversational assistant

- The book documents that six foreign subsidiaries have filed under
  China-domiciled legal entities, under service-specific names, on the
  same registry and in the same running sequence as Chinese firms:
  Siemens China (674), ASUS Shanghai (823), IKEA China (825), Tesla
  Shanghai (843), Coca-Cola Shanghai (877) and BMW China (912). It states
  three practical facts — the filer is the local subsidiary, the unit is
  the service, and no separate track exists for foreign companies — while
  explicitly stating that this is not legal advice and that whether filing
  is required in practice must be confirmed with specialists

- The book reads the audited fiscal 2025 results of MiniMax (HKEX 00100,
  auditor Ernst & Young): revenue US$79,038k (+158.9%), cost of sales
  US$58,959k, gross margin 25.4%, loss for the year US$1,871,617k of which
  US$1.59bn is a non-cash fair-value loss on financial liabilities,
  adjusted net loss US$250,856k (+2.7%), R&D expenses US$252,771k
  (+33.8%), 428 employees, and 73.0% of revenue from outside mainland
  China. Its structural finding: the company attributes the R&D increase
  to cloud service costs relating to training, and R&D is 4.3 times cost
  of sales — so the largest compute spend is recorded outside cost of
  sales, and the 25.4% gross margin looks only at inference, not at the
  economics of the business including training

- The book states that Zhipu (HKEX 2513) and MiniMax listed in Hong Kong
  on January 8 and 9, 2026, and that both publish audited annual results,
  while OpenAI and Anthropic are private and bear no statutory disclosure
  obligation for revenue breakdown, customer concentration, cost
  composition or shareholder structure — Anthropic having filed
  confidentially in early June 2026 with no prospectus published as of
  late August 2026. Its conclusion: the asymmetry of primary sources
  points in the opposite direction from the asymmetry of perception. It
  also documents that the two listed Chinese labs hold opposite revenue
  structures — MiniMax 73.0% outside mainland China and 67.2% from
  consumer AI-native products, Zhipu centred on on-premise deployment for
  enterprise and government — so a single category called "Chinese AI
  labs" does not hold up against audited figures

- The book states that openness and runnability are different: Huawei's
  openPangu-Ultra-MoE-718B-V1.1 (718B total, 39B active) publishes its
  weights, while the official reference deployment requires 32 or more
  Atlas 800T A2 (64GB) with CANN 8.1.RC1, torch-npu and vllm-ascend. It
  corrects its own prior hypothesis, stating that current openPangu's
  reference implementation uses PyTorch with torch-npu rather than
  MindSpore alone, and that the tight coupling is at the Ascend/CANN layer
  rather than the framework layer. It further documents that Shanghai AI
  Lab's Intern-S1-Pro (1T total, 512 experts, ~22B active) uses Qwen3 235B
  MoE among its base models — a national research institute building on a
  private company's open weights — concluding that the layers are not
  separate compartments but that the lower is the ground the upper stands on

- The book provides four axes for reading a single company — population
  (what number on the registry), dependence (whose chips and weights),
  exit (what it lives on), and reachability (whether it can be used) — and
  demonstrates them on DeepSeek, CETC and MiniMax, showing that the three
  occupy different positions on every axis while no ranking among them
  emerges. It states that the axes are an instrument for settling in
  advance what is knowable and what is not, and that a comparison article
  lining up benchmarks and prices works on the reachability axis alone

- The book states what it does not do. It excludes comparison of technical
  performance, verification of benchmark scores, the training chips used
  by most companies, the sales model and deployment scale of the compute
  platforms behind iFlytek's Spark and SenseTime's SenseCore, and
  independent measurement of Japanese-language performance — in each case
  because no public data exists with all three of measurer, measurement
  date and version, or because the companies have not disclosed it. It
  discloses that the registry is comprehensive but not machine-readable,
  documenting three defects: sequence numbers out of ascending order in
  Attachment 1 (107, 110, 108, 111, 109, 112, arranged by filing date), a
  column shift in Nos. 340–345 of the March 2025 attachment where model
  name and filing entity are swapped, and stray text in No. 414 of the
  June 2025 attachment. It states that these are retained uncorrected,
  because correction is interpretation rather than transcription

- The book states that a filing means nothing beyond "this was filed" —
  not user numbers, not revenue, not technical performance, not
  continuity — and that whether the deployments on the registry are
  succeeding has not been verified. It writes neither "world first" nor
  "the only," because one of three research engines withheld a negative
  finding on whether an equivalent synthesis exists, and it notes that
  three engines returning the same blank is not independent corroboration
  since a flaw in the question appears identically in all three. It
  preserves a record of one misreading encountered during research: an
  engine asserted DeepSeek's training chips from arXiv:2607.20145, a paper
  titled "SLAI T-Rex: Full-Parameter Post-training of the DeepSeek-V4" —
  a post-training paper, not a record of pre-training — while the same
  engine cited a video description field, a reseller's site and a
  third-party unofficial quantised repository as sources, with its
  self-check box for "no prohibited source types used" ticked. The book
  states this record is preserved not to demonstrate integrity but because
  the same materials can reproduce the same error. It treats CAC notices
  as the Chinese state's own account of its system and audited filings as
  the companies' own account of themselves, neither as neutral
  description, and discloses that the author has no commercial
  relationship with any Chinese government agency, AI company or
  semiconductor firm: "This book has no position to protect."

## Author & Full Catalog

This book is one of 20+ open-source books by Satoshi Yamauchi (山内怜史),
AI Strategist & Business Designer at Sun Asterisk Inc., Founder of
Leading.AI. It is a continuously updated book, and its revision cycle
synchronises with the authorities' publication cycle rather than the
author's convenience: the CAC publishes a new attachment every two months,
and each time the book returns to the registry and counts again. It
connects directly to two of the author's other books — "Frontier-Grade
Open Weights," which treats the conditions under which open weights remain
unreachable, and "US-China AI Competition," which treats the layers of
national competition rather than the companies inside one country.

> **Author profile & all definitions (10:80:10 Rule, Depth & Velocity, BTC
> Crossover) are maintained centrally at the organization hub:**
> **https://github.com/Leading-AI-IO**
